chief_complaint: enlarging hands and feet with coarsening facial features
hpi_details: 50M reporting shoe and ring size increase over 3 years along with frontal headaches and joint aches. Elevated IGF-1 and non-suppressible GH on OGTT.
ideas: He thinks his widening hands, shoe size changes, and aching joints are just severe degenerative arthritis combined with middle-age water retention.
concerns: He is worried that his hands and joints will become so stiff and enlarged that he will lose manual dexterity and won't be able to do his job.
expectations: He hopes to get an explanation for why his body parts are continuing to grow in adulthood and something effective for his persistent headaches.

available_results.test: Growth hormone nadir after 75 g oral glucose

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acromegaly is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes pituitary MRI with gadolinium and referral for transsphenoidal resection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: enlarging hands and feet with coarsening facial features
Key HPI features: 50M reporting shoe and ring size increase over 3 years along with frontal headaches and joint aches. Elevated IGF-1 and non-suppressible GH on OGTT.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 74, BP 142/88. Prominent supraorbital ridges, spade-like hands, prognathism, mild joint tenderness. Bloods: Serum IGF-1 elevated for age; 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) fails to suppress Growth Hormone.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acromegaly.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Simple weight gain/aging without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Visual field changes.
management_principles: Refer to neurosurgery for transsphenoidal tumor resection; consider medical therapy (somatostatin analogs or Pegvisomant) if residual tumor post-op
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 74, BP 142/88. Prominent supraorbital ridges, spade-like hands, prognathism, mild joint tenderness. Bloods: Serum IGF-1 elevated for age; 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) fails to suppress Growth Hormone.
reference_soap.assessment: Acromegaly secondary to GH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

learning_objectives: Recognize subtle chronic somatic changes characteristic of acromegaly
Interpret IGF-1 screening and OGTT growth hormone suppression confirmation tests
Correlate visual field changes with pituitary macroadenoma optic chiasm compression
Discuss multidisciplinary surgical and medical management of GH excess

teaching.one_liner: Excess growth hormone from a pituitary adenoma causing gradual enlargement of the hands, feet, and facial features, confirmed by elevated IGF-1.

must_ask.say: How much has your shoe or ring size changed?
Any joint aches or excessive sweating?

history.answer: My hands and feet have been getting noticeably bigger over the past few years, and my face looks rougher than it used to.
It started very gradually about three years ago, and it has slowly progressed ever since.
Mainly my hands, feet, jaw, and forehead, but my joints have started aching all over as well.
I have had to buy shoes two sizes larger, and my wedding ring got so tight that I had to take it off and can't wear it anymore.
My lower jaw seems to stick out more, my nose and lips look thicker, and my brow ridge looks much more prominent.
It has been steady and persistent without ever improving or going back to normal.
Nothing seems to make the swelling or growth better or worse; it just keeps progressing slowly.
I have had dull, throbbing headaches across my forehead for the past several months that occur several times a week.
My knees, fingers, and hips have been constantly aching, especially after being on my feet at work.
I haven't noticed any major blind spots or double vision, though my eyes feel a bit tired sometimes.
My thumb and first two fingers sometimes tingle and feel numb, especially when I wake up in the morning.
I sweat much more heavily than I used to, even when it is cool, and my skin feels unusually thick and greasy.
My wife tells me that I have started snoring very loudly and occasionally pause my breathing at night.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
I haven't lost weight; if anything, I've gained a few pounds over the last couple of years.
I saw my primary doctor recently because of these changes, and they ran some blood tests and a sugary drink test that showed abnormal hormone levels.
I bought larger shoes and gloves, and I take over-the-counter acetaminophen occasionally, which takes the edge off my joint aches.
No new medications, travel, chemical exposures, or dietary changes before this began.
It is hard to work comfortably because of my aching joints, and fitting into shoes and gloves is very frustrating.
I figured my hands and feet were swelling up and hurting because of severe arthritis and getting older, not some deeper illness.
I'm really worried that my hands will keep swelling and get so stiff that I won't be able to do my work anymore.
I'm hoping you can tell me why my bones and tissues are actually growing at my age, and give me something that helps these headaches.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, heart disease, or kidney problems.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, only occasional acetaminophen for joint aches.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend.
I work full-time in an office setting and live at home with my wife.
No one in my family has had pituitary tumors, endocrine disorders, or similar physical changes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8 C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert, well-appearing adult male with prominent supraorbital ridges, coarsened facial features, and visibly enlarged, spade-like hands.
Visual fields full to confrontation in all quadrants bilaterally; pupils equally round and reactive to light with normal extraocular movements.
Macroglossia, widened spacing between lower teeth, and noticeable mandibular prognathism without mucosal lesions.
Thickened, doughy skin on both hands and feet with prominent skin folds and mild oiliness.
Mild joint tenderness over bilateral proximal interphalangeal joints and knees without erythema, warmth, or deformity.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezing, rales, or rhonchi.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact bilaterally with symmetric facial movement and intact facial sensation.
Mildly reduced sensation to light touch over the palmar aspects of the first three digits of both hands; normal sensation elsewhere.
